Moving data

Transformers

A connector moves bytes. A transformer turns them into Arrow RecordBatch and back. Five formats ship with PCS, csv, ndjson, parquet, avro and arrow-ipc, and a transformer node picks one by name.

In one line
Transport and byte format are separate crates, chosen separately
You need
The transformer crate for a Rust pipeline; on pcs-service, its transformer-* feature as well
Read this if
You are declaring a transformer node, or teaching PCS a format it does not ship

Connector against transformer

A connector owns a transport. FileSource opens the path, drives one OS thread and pushes batches down a bounded channel of four, so the file is never materialised in full. TcpIngestSource owns the listener and the frame length prefix, KafkaSource owns the consumer group. None of them reads a byte's meaning.

A transformer owns a byte format. It knows nothing about paths, sockets or topics, so NdjsonTransformer decodes the same rows whether the bytes arrived from a disk, a socket or a Kafka topic. The contract lives in pcs-transformer, below every connector, and each format is its own crate.

bytes and batches the format boundary

Declaring a transformer

A workflow declares each byte format it needs as its own transformer node. The node's leading argument is its id, format names the registered format, and an options child is the table handed to that format's factory. Every source or sink that moves bytes names one declared transformer through its own transformer key.

There is no default and no format sniffing: a file connector does not read the extension, and Kafka, NATS and TCP each name a transformer like everything else.

KDLoptions belongs to the format, the transformer key to the node; both nodes sit inside one workflow
transformer "orders_csv" format="csv" {
    options has_headers=#true
}

source "orders_in" type="FileSource" component="Order" transformer="orders_csv" {
    config path="/data/orders.csv" {
        schema_fields "id" type="Int64" nullable=#false
    }
}

Each format defines its own options keys, and its page lists them with their defaults. Omit the node and every option keeps its default. Two transformer nodes may name the same format with different options, so one workflow reads Confluent framed Avro on one topic and single-object Avro on another.

What each format can do

A transformer has two surfaces. The stream surface, open_reader and open_writer, is what the file, HTTP and S3 connectors use. The message surface, open_message_decoder and encode_messages, is what Kafka, NATS and TCP use. All five formats implement both, so no format is refused for lacking a surface; a format that implemented only one would be a configuration error naming the format and the capability.

Every connector settles that at build time. A message sink gates on message_shape, which answers for both directions, and a tcp source opens a decoder off the declared schema inside its constructor, so pcs-service validate is where a mismatch surfaces rather than the first connection.

formatStream readStream writeMessage codecMessage shapeDeclared schemaCrate
csv yes yes yes PerRow required pcs-transformer-csv
ndjson yes yes yes PerRow optional pcs-transformer-ndjson
parquet yes yes yes PerBatch refused reading a file, required writing and on messages pcs-transformer-parquet
avro yes yes yes PerRow refused reading a file, required writing and on messages pcs-transformer-avro
arrow-ipc yes yes yes PerBatch refused reading a stream, required writing and on messages pcs-transformer-arrow-ipc

arrow-ipc and parquet each use one encapsulation on both surfaces, so a file written by a FileSink decodes through the message decoder and one Kafka payload opens as a reader. A parquet payload is a whole file, footer included: about 470 bytes of fixed cost for a three-column row type before any data, which is why its shape is PerBatch. parquet is also the only format that reports estimated_rows, summed from row-group metadata without reading any data.

csv's has_headers option governs the stream surface alone. A message is one record with no header line, in either direction, because the decoder is handed the declared schema and needs no column names.

MessageShape decides how a batch splits on the way out. PerRow emits one message per row, which is what a Kafka key_field needs to have a key to pair each payload with. PerBatch emits one message carrying the whole batch. On the message surface avro reads single-object framing always, and Confluent framing when options schema_id names the registry id, so one stream may carry both.

The Declared schema column is about a source. A FileSink requires schema_fields whatever the format, because that is the schema the rows are written with.

The traits

pcs-transformer holds five traits and one enum. Four of them are below, and TransformerFactory is under Writing your own. Only format has no default: a transformer implements the surfaces it has and inherits an unsupported error for the rest. Both readers and writers are synchronous, because the connector owns the thread and the async plumbing.

Rustevery method with a default returns unsupported
// pcs-transformer
pub trait Transformer: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn format(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn open_reader(&self, input: std::fs::File, declared: Option<Arc<Schema>>)
        -> Result<Box<dyn BatchReader>, PcsError>;      // defaults to `unsupported`
    fn open_writer(&self, output: Box<dyn std::io::Write + Send>, schema: Arc<Schema>)
        -> Result<Box<dyn BatchWriter>, PcsError>;      // defaults to `unsupported`
    fn open_message_decoder(&self, schema: Arc<Schema>)
        -> Result<Box<dyn MessageDecoder>, PcsError>;   // defaults to `unsupported`
    fn encode_messages(&self, batch: &RecordBatch)
        -> Result<Vec<Vec<u8>>, PcsError>;              // defaults to `unsupported`
    fn message_shape(&self) -> Option<MessageShape>;    // defaults to None
}

pub trait BatchReader: Send {
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema>;
    fn next_batch(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, PcsError>;
    fn estimated_rows(&self) -> Option<usize>;          // defaults to None
}

pub trait BatchWriter: Send {
    fn write_batch(&mut self, batch: &RecordBatch) -> Result<(), PcsError>;
    fn finish(self: Box<Self>) -> Result<(), PcsError>;
}

pub trait MessageDecoder: Send {
    fn push(&mut self, payload: &[u8]) -> Result<(), PcsError>;
    fn flush(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, PcsError>;
}

pub enum MessageShape { PerRow, PerBatch }

Message encoding is Transformer::encode_messages itself, so there is no encoder trait to implement. BatchWriter::finish consumes the writer, so a format with a footer cannot be written to afterwards. MessageDecoder::flush resets the decoder, so one decoder serves a whole TCP connection or Kafka consumer.

Writing your own

An out-of-tree transformer is a crate that depends on pcs-core for PcsError and pcs-transformer for the traits, and on nothing else of PCS: no connector, no host. Implement Transformer for the codec and TransformerFactory for the name a format key selects it with.

Rustthe factory reads options, the transformer it builds is shared
// pcs-transformer
pub trait TransformerFactory: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn format_name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn build(&self, options: &ConfigValue) -> Result<Arc<dyn Transformer>, PcsError>;
}

// in a custom binary
let builder = register_builtin_factories(ServiceBuilder::new())
    .register_transformer(ProtobufTransformerFactory);

ServiceBuilder::register_transformer installs it, and from then on transformer "p" format="protobuf" resolves, with no change to any connector. Registering a format_name that is already taken replaces the earlier factory, so a custom csv can stand in for the built-in one.

Features

On pcs-service, one feature per transformer decides what register_builtin_factories installs: transformer-csv, transformer-ndjson, transformer-parquet, transformer-avro and transformer-arrow-ipc. connector-kafka and connector-nats each pull in transformer-ndjson and connector-tcp pulls in transformer-arrow-ipc, so any one of the three is runnable on its own.

Bashconnector-file implies no transformer, so pick one
cargo build --features connector-file,transformer-csv,wasm
Sharp edge

A format the build does not carry fails loudly rather than falling back: transformer 'orders_json' names format 'parquet', which no transformer is registered for (registered: csv, ndjson). The registry holds exactly what the features compiled in, so the fix is a feature or a register_transformer call.
